summary: Stocks enter Thanksgiving week in a correction. The S&P 500 fell 3.7% Friday to 6,910 and lost 8.6% on the week, its worst since April 2025, while the Nasdaq fell 10% and the Dow lost 8%. Nvidia dropped 14% Friday after Reuters reported that regulators were examining its accounting, and chip stocks fell hard with it. Money moved into Treasuries, with the 10 year yield down to about 4.9% from 5.15% a week earlier, and the VIX closed near 36. Almost all of the US data lands Wednesday morning, led by October PCE, the last major inflation report before the December 8 to 9 Fed meeting. Dell on Tuesday night is the first big test of AI spending since the rout. US markets are closed Thursday, and on Friday stocks close at 1:00 PM ET and bonds at 2:00 PM ET.

stats.label: December hike odds
stats.sub: Quarter point, CME FedWatch at Friday's close. 8% hold, 0% for a half point

headline.title: Wednesday Nov 25: PCE inflation, GDP, durable goods, claims and the Beige Book
headline.body: Six US releases land between 8:30 AM and 2:00 PM ET on the last full session before Thanksgiving. Core PCE is expected at 0.3% for the month and 3.2% for the year, up from 3.1%. With stocks in a correction and December hike odds slipping to about 92%, the question is whether inflation is firm enough to keep the Fed hiking into a falling market. Expect thinner holiday trading, which can exaggerate moves.

spotlight.name: Dell Technologies
spotlight.when: Tue Nov 24, after the close, call 4:30 PM ET
spotlight.watch: AI server demand, how much of the record $95B AI backlog turns into sales, and margins. Dell guided to about $49B and 6.50. Options were pricing a swing of about 12.7%.

spotlight.name: Analog Devices
spotlight.when: Tue Nov 24, before the open, release 7:00 AM ET
spotlight.watch: Whether industrial, auto and data center demand is still strengthening after the worst week for chip stocks in years. Revenue is expected to rise about 40% from a year ago.

spotlight.name: Deere
spotlight.when: Wed Nov 25, before the open, call 10:00 AM ET
spotlight.watch: The fiscal 2027 outlook. Deere has said 2026 marks the bottom of the farm equipment cycle, so a cautious guide would be the main risk.

macro.name: Chicago Fed National Activity Index (Oct)
macro.note: A composite of 85 indicators that shows whether the economy is growing above or below trend.
macro.react: Rarely moves markets. A clearly negative reading would fit the recent soft factory surveys and give bonds a small lift.

macro.name: S&P Global flash PMIs (Nov)
macro.note: The first broad look at November business activity. October factory activity was the best since 2022, but prices also jumped. Watch the price components.
macro.react: Strong activity with hot prices would lift yields and the dollar and could add to the pressure on tech. A moderate slowdown with softer prices would be the friendliest mix for stocks and bonds. A sharp drop could stir growth worries in a market that is already nervous.

macro.name: 2 year Treasury auction ($69B)
macro.note: A day earlier than usual because of the holiday. The 2 year yield ended last week near 4.65% after a large drop.
macro.react: Strong demand would confirm the move into safe assets and help rate sensitive stocks. Weak demand would push short yields back up and hint that the rally has gone too far.

macro.name: Fed speaker: Williams (New York Fed)
macro.note: The only scheduled Fed speaker found for the week, and a permanent voter. The Fed goes quiet from midnight Saturday ahead of the December meeting. He recently said more hikes will likely be needed.
macro.react: If he repeats the call for hikes and plays down the selloff, short yields and the dollar could rise and tech could stay under pressure. Any mention of tighter financial conditions would be read as a door opening to a hold, which would help growth stocks and small caps. About 92% odds of a quarter point hike are already priced.

macro.name: Global: eurozone, Germany and UK flash PMIs (Nov)
macro.note: Early November activity in Europe, released between about 3:30 and 4:30 AM ET.
macro.react: Firm readings would support the euro and pound and lift European yields, which can spill into Treasuries. Weak readings would add to global growth worries before the US open.

macro.name: ADP weekly employment change
macro.note: A frequent read on private hiring. The last reading was the strongest since September. The prior shown covers the four weeks ending October 31.
macro.react: A strong number would support the view that the job market can handle a hike and nudge yields up. A sharp drop would help bonds. It usually has a small effect.

macro.name: Case Shiller home prices and FHFA index (Sep)
macro.note: Lagged home price data. Housing is weak with mortgage rates above 7%.
macro.react: Little effect on the broad market. A softer reading would weigh on homebuilders, though it would also point to cooler housing inflation later.

macro.name: Conference Board consumer confidence (Nov)
macro.note: How households feel about jobs and income heading into the holidays. Part of the survey window may miss the worst of the stock drop.
macro.react: A solid reading would support retailers before Black Friday but keep the hike on track. A large miss would hit consumer discretionary names and lift bonds, since stock losses could be starting to dent spending. The jobs questions matter most.

macro.name: Richmond Fed manufacturing survey (Nov)
macro.note: Factory conditions in the mid Atlantic states, following weak surveys from New York and Philadelphia.
macro.react: Another weak reading would add to signs of a factory slowdown and help bonds slightly. Watch the prices paid measure.

macro.name: 5 year Treasury auction ($70B)
macro.note: The second of three note sales this week.
macro.react: A weak auction would lift yields across the curve and weigh on growth stocks. Strong demand would extend the rally in bonds.

macro.name: Global: Germany Ifo survey (Nov) and Australia CPI (Oct)
macro.note: Ifo is due around 4:00 AM ET. Australia's monthly inflation lands around 7:30 PM ET.
macro.react: A hot Australian print would add to the global theme of rising rates and support the Australian dollar. Ifo rarely moves US markets.

macro.name: PCE inflation, personal income and spending (Oct)
macro.cons: Core PCE 0.3% m/m, 3.2% y/y. Headline 0.3% m/m, 3.8% y/y. Income 0.4%, spending 0.4%
macro.prior: Core 0.3% m/m, 3.1% y/y. Headline 0.5% m/m, 3.6% y/y. Income 0.2%, spending 0.5%
macro.note: The Fed's preferred inflation gauge. Forecasts come from CPI and PPI, so most of the number is already known. The Cleveland Fed nowcast matches consensus.
macro.react: A core reading of 0.4% would push hike odds back toward 100%, revive talk of a half point and lift the 2 year yield and the dollar, with tech and small caps most exposed. A 0.2% would lower yields and help growth stocks, homebuilders and gold. An in line number is already priced and would likely shift attention back to the selloff itself.

macro.name: GDP second estimate and corporate profits (Q3)
macro.note: An update of third quarter growth plus the first look at profits. Second quarter growth was 2.2%. Watch consumer spending and the price measures.
macro.react: An upward revision with firm prices would support more hikes and lift yields. A downgrade to consumer spending would help bonds but worry cyclical stocks. Usually secondary to PCE at the same time.

macro.name: Initial jobless claims (week of Nov 21)
macro.note: Moved up a day for Thanksgiving. Continuing claims rose to 1.763 million, the highest since late August.
macro.react: Claims near 200,000 would confirm a tight job market and keep the hike on track. A jump above 215,000 or another rise in continuing claims would rally bonds and lower hike odds. Holiday weeks can be noisy.

macro.name: Durable goods orders (Oct)
macro.note: Orders for long lasting goods. Core capital goods orders are a window into business and AI equipment spending.
macro.react: Strong core orders would calm fears that AI spending is cracking and help industrials and chip equipment. A weak reading would add to the AI worry and weigh on both. Aircraft orders can distort the headline.

macro.name: New home sales (Oct)
macro.note: Sales of newly built homes with mortgage rates above 7%. Builder confidence just hit its lowest since 2012.
macro.react: A miss would weigh on homebuilders but help bonds. A surprise gain would support builders and home improvement names. Limited effect on the broad market.

macro.name: 7 year Treasury auction ($44B)
macro.note: The last note sale of the week, in thin trading before the holiday.
macro.react: A poor auction in thin markets could lift long yields quickly. Good demand would support the safe haven trade.

macro.name: Fed Beige Book
macro.note: Stories from businesses in all 12 Fed districts, prepared for the December meeting. Watch comments on prices, hiring, tariffs and AI spending.
macro.react: Wider reports of price increases would back a hike and lift short yields. More mentions of weak demand or slower hiring would help the case for patience and support growth stocks.

macro.name: Bank of Korea rate decision
macro.cons: Hike to 3.25%, some expect a hold
macro.note: Announced Thursday morning local time. A survey of 20 experts found 90% expect a hike this month.
macro.react: A hike would support the won and add to the global tightening story. A surprise hold would help Korean stocks, including memory chip names, which could lift US chip sentiment in holiday trading.

macro.name: US stock and bond markets closed for Thanksgiving
macro.note: No US trading and no US data. Retailers and card companies start to share early holiday sales numbers through the weekend.
macro.react: Overseas markets stay open, so news can build up and show as a gap on Friday morning. With the VIX near 36, hedges held over the closure carry more risk than in a normal holiday week.

macro.name: ECB account of the October meeting
macro.note: Minutes style summary of the European Central Bank's last policy discussion.
macro.react: A hawkish tone would lift the euro and European yields. A cautious one would do the opposite. US cash markets cannot react until Friday.

macro.name: Global: Tokyo CPI (Nov), China industrial profits (Oct), Bank of England stability report
macro.cons: Not found for Tokyo CPI and China profits
macro.note: Tokyo inflation is due around 6:30 PM ET and China profits around 8:30 PM ET. The Bank of England report is due around 5:30 AM ET and may address risks from high AI stock prices.
macro.react: A hot Tokyo print would raise odds of Bank of Japan tightening and lift the yen, which can pressure leveraged trades funded in yen and weigh on tech. Soft China profits would weigh on copper and miners.

macro.name: Advance goods trade, wholesale and retail inventories (Oct)
macro.note: Early inputs for fourth quarter growth forecasts. AI equipment imports have been a large part of the deficit.
macro.react: A smaller deficit would lift fourth quarter growth estimates and firm yields slightly. A wider one would trim them. Reaction is usually small, and thin trading can exaggerate it.

macro.name: Early close: stocks at 1:00 PM ET, bonds at 2:00 PM ET
macro.note: Black Friday half day. Expect light volume. The first headlines on holiday traffic and online sales arrive during the session.
macro.react: Strong early sales would help retailers, payment names and Amazon. Weak traffic would raise doubts about the consumer after the stock drop. Moves on thin volume often fade on Monday.

macro.name: Global: France and Spain CPI (Nov), eurozone sentiment, Germany unemployment
macro.cons: Eurozone sentiment 97.1. Germany unemployment rate 6.4%. Deutsche Bank sees France 3.53% and Spain 4.57%
macro.note: First November inflation numbers from Europe, due between about 2:45 and 5:00 AM ET. Spain and France set the tone for the eurozone figure the following week.
macro.react: Hot prints would lift European yields and the euro and could pull Treasury yields higher in thin trading. Softer prints would ease global rate worries and help growth stocks.

notes: Earnings shows large market cap names and widely traded movers, not every report. EPS figures are consensus estimates from Robinhood data and can differ from other sources, since some providers use adjusted and others use reported figures. The gap is wide for Zoom, Autodesk, Workday, Bilibili and Li Auto. Spotlight ranges combine Robinhood with public previews.

Consensus figures come from public week ahead previews and can change. Where sources differ, a range is shown. Figures not confirmed are marked Not found. Reports scheduled for the following week, such as Marvell on December 1, are left out.
Reaction notes are scenario thinking, not predictions.
